title: Complete Multiplicativity Structure
content: This file answers the open question from OQ-03: can the Jacobi symbol reciprocity proof be completed by finding the right Mathlib API calls? The answer is definitively YES. Mathlib's jacobiSym module provides complete multiplicativity in both arguments, periodicity, power laws, coprimality characterization, and special reciprocity forms. This file catalogs and connects all these properties, showing they form a complete system for computing any Jacobi symbol value.
mathContext: The Jacobi symbol $J(\cdot, n)$ is a completely multiplicative function $\mathbb{Z} \to \{-1, 0, 1\}$ that factors through $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Top-Argument Complete Multiplicativity
content: The Jacobi symbol is completely multiplicative in its first argument: J(a1*a2, n) = J(a1, n) * J(a2, n) for ALL integers a1, a2 and natural number n. This is stronger than the bottom-argument multiplicativity (which requires nonzero arguments). Complete multiplicativity means the Jacobi symbol is determined by its values on primes and -1, which is exactly what QR and the supplements provide.
mathContext: $J(a_1 a_2, n) = J(a_1, n) \cdot J(a_2, n)$ for all $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$. No coprimality or parity hypotheses needed.
prerequisites: definition of Jacobi symbol via prime factorization

title: Periodicity: The Key Reduction Step
content: J(a, n) = J(a mod n, n) is the single most important computational property. It means the Jacobi symbol factors through Z/nZ, so we never need to work with integers larger than n. Combined with QR (which swaps the arguments), this creates a Euclidean-like descent: reduce a mod n, swap via QR, reduce again. Each step shrinks the problem, guaranteeing termination.
mathContext: $J(a, n) = J(a \bmod n, n)$. The symbol depends only on the residue class $a + n\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Power Laws and Square Detection
content: The power laws J(a^k, n) = J(a,n)^k and J(a, n^k) = J(a,n)^k follow directly from multiplicativity. The key corollary is J(a^2, n) = 1 for coprime a,n — perfect squares always have Jacobi symbol 1. This is the basis for the Solovay-Strassen test: if J(a,n) != a^((n-1)/2) mod n, then n is composite.
mathContext: $J(a^k, n) = J(a, n)^k$ and $J(a, n^k) = J(a, n)^k$. In particular, $J(a^2, n) = 1$ when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

title: Coprimality Characterization and Trichotomy
content: The vanishing criterion J(a,n) = 0 iff gcd(a,n) > 1 (and n != 0) gives a complete partition of the domain. For coprime inputs, J takes values in {+1, -1}. For non-coprime inputs, J = 0. This trichotomy {-1, 0, 1} is the full image of the Jacobi symbol, and each value has a clear number-theoretic meaning: -1 = guaranteed non-residue, 0 = not coprime, 1 = possibly residue (certainly for prime moduli).
mathContext: $J(a, n) = 0 \iff n \neq 0 \land \gcd(a, n) > 1$. When $\gcd(a, n) = 1$: $J(a, n) \in \{\pm 1\}$.

title: Special Reciprocity: Simplified Cases
content: When a ≡ 1 (mod 4), the sign factor (-1)^((a-1)/2 * (n-1)/2) equals 1 (since (a-1)/2 is even), giving the clean identity J(a,n) = J(n,a). When both a,n ≡ 3 (mod 4), the sign factor is -1, giving J(a,n) = -J(n,a). These simplifications accelerate the Euclidean algorithm — about half of all reciprocity flips are sign-free.
mathContext: If $a \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$: $J(a, n) = J(n, a)$. If $a \equiv n \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$: $J(a, n) = -J(n, a)$.

title: Euclidean Reduction Algorithm
content: The three formalized reduction steps — (1) reduce top mod bottom, (2) extract factors of 2, (3) apply QR to swap — constitute the Jacobi symbol computation algorithm. Each iteration reduces the problem size (like the Euclidean algorithm for GCD), guaranteeing termination. The supplements J(-1,n) = chi_4(n) and J(2,n) = chi_8(n) handle the base cases after all reductions. This algorithm runs in O(log^2 n) time, matching GCD computation complexity.
mathContext: Algorithm: $J(a,n) \xrightarrow{\text{mod}} J(a', n) \xrightarrow{\text{factor 2}} J(2,n)^k \cdot J(a'', n) \xrightarrow{\text{QR}} \pm J(n, a'') \to \cdots$

title: Computational Verifications
content: Nine concrete examples verified by native_decide demonstrate the multiplicative structure in action. Key examples: (1) J(2,15) = J(2,3)*J(2,5) = (-1)*(-1) = 1 shows bottom multiplicativity; (2) J(6,35) = J(2,35)*J(3,35) shows top multiplicativity; (3) J(4,15) = J(2^2,15) = 1 shows the square property; (4) J(17,15) = J(2,15) shows periodicity; (5) J(1001,9907) = J(7,9907)*J(11,9907)*J(13,9907) shows factorization via mul_left.
